claims.text: Thermally activated segregation of reactive elements toward the surface is the primary cause of protective oxide development and retention in high-entropy alloys.
The relevant high-entropy alloys initially have a homogeneous distribution of reactive elements.
High-temperature exposure thermally activates selective diffusion of Al, Cr, or Si toward the alloy surface.
Reactive-element segregation produces a near-surface concentration gradient.
The near-surface reactive-element gradient enables growth of a graded protective oxide scale.
Surface-enriched Al, Cr, or Si oxidizes preferentially.
Preferential oxidation of surface-segregated reactive elements forms a continuous oxide film.
Preferential oxidation of surface-segregated reactive elements forms an adherent oxide film.
The resulting oxide film acts as an oxygen-diffusion barrier.
The oxygen-diffusion barrier retards further oxidation.
Enhancing reactive-element surface segregation will produce thinner oxide scales than suppressing segregation.
Enhancing reactive-element surface segregation will produce more uniform oxide scales than suppressing segregation.
Enhancing reactive-element surface segregation will produce more adherent oxide scales than suppressing segregation.
Enhancing reactive-element surface segregation will reduce oxidation kinetics, weight gain, and oxide-scale growth rate relative to suppressed segregation.
Uniform or inhibited reactive-element distributions are expected to produce porous or non-uniform, less-protective oxide scales.
Uniform or inhibited reactive-element distributions are expected to result in higher oxidation rates.
The proposed mechanism is effective only when the alloy contains sufficient reactive elements.
Extremely high oxygen pressure or significant contaminants may invalidate or substantially alter the proposed segregation-controlled mechanism.
